overview.title: A model too small to overfit
overview.main_topic: Diagnosing insufficient model capacity using a single-layer logistic regression on MNIST
overview.central_idea: A one-layer softmax classifier (logistic regression) on raw MNIST pixels trains, but its validation loss flattens around 0.26 and never turns upward: it cannot overfit, which is the signature of too little capacity.
overview.importance: The book's workflow says you should first reach a model that can overfit. This page shows what the curves look like when you cannot get there, so you can recognize the situation in your own projects and know the fix is a bigger model.
learning_objectives: Read Listing 5.9 and explain why a single Dense(10, softmax) layer is a multiclass logistic regression.
Explain the role of validation_split=0.2 and of the History object returned by fit().
Plot a validation-loss curve from history.history with Matplotlib.
Recognize the 'stall' shape of Figure 5.14 as a sign of insufficient capacity, as opposed to the 'U' shape of overfitting.
prerequisites: The MNIST setup with train_images reshaped to (60000, 784) and scaled to [0, 1] (chapter 2 and earlier in chapter 5).
Softmax output and sparse categorical crossentropy (chapter 2).
Underfitting vs. overfitting and the shape of validation curves (section 5.1, p.161).

summary:
Section 5.3.3 opens with a deliberately weak model. **Listing 5.9** builds `keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])`: a single dense layer that maps the 784 pixel values of each MNIST image directly to 10 class probabilities. The book calls it what it is, *a simple logistic regression* (strictly, multinomial or softmax logistic regression). It is compiled with `rmsprop`, `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` and an accuracy metric, then trained for 20 epochs with batches of 128, holding out the last 20% of the training data as validation data via `validation_split=0.2`. The `History` object is stored in `history_small_model`.

A second snippet uses Matplotlib to plot `history_small_model.history["val_loss"]` against epochs 1 to 20, producing **Figure 5.14**, "Effect of insufficient model capacity on loss curves". The curve drops quickly from about 0.36 after the first epoch, then flattens: by about epoch 10 it is near 0.267 and it ends around 0.26.

The text interprets the shape. Validation metrics *stall or improve very slowly* instead of **peaking and reversing course**, which is what overfitting looks like. The loss "goes to 0.26 and just stays there." The sentence continues on p.181: you can fit, but you cannot clearly overfit, however long you train. The book then argues it should always be possible to overfit, and that the fix is more representational power: more layers, bigger layers, or better-suited layer types.

The lesson for practice: a curve that never turns upward is not good news. It means the model has too little capacity to memorize the training data, so it is also leaving generalization performance unused.

paragraphs.excerpt: Consider the following small model—a simple logistic regression—trained on MNIST pixels.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduces Listing 5.9 as a small model, specifically a logistic regression, trained directly on MNIST pixel values.
paragraphs.what_it_means: One Dense layer with 10 softmax units and no hidden layers is exactly multinomial logistic regression. Each class score is a weighted sum of the 784 pixels plus a bias, and softmax turns the 10 scores into probabilities. Its decision boundaries between classes are linear in pixel space.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Choosing a linear model is deliberate: it is the clearest possible case of a model with too little capacity, which section 5.3.3 needs as its starting example.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the model has 784×10 + 10 = 7,850 trainable parameters. A linear classifier on raw MNIST pixels typically reaches about 92% test accuracy and plateaus there.

terminology.meaning: A linear classifier that maps a weighted sum of the inputs to class probabilities: through a sigmoid for two classes, through a softmax for several (multinomial logistic regression).
The 28×28 grayscale digit images, flattened to 784-dimensional vectors scaled to [0, 1].

connections: p.179: section 5.3.3 'Increasing model capacity' begins on the previous page
p.181: the same task is retrained with two 128-unit hidden layers for comparison

paragraphs.excerpt: Validation metrics seem to stall or to improve very slowly, instead of peaking
paragraphs.what_it_says: Figure 5.14 shows validation metrics that stall or improve very slowly instead of peaking and then getting worse. The validation loss reaches 0.26 and stays there. The sentence 'You can fit, but…' continues on p.181: '…you can't clearly overfit, even after many iterations over the training data.'
paragraphs.what_it_means: A model with enough capacity eventually memorizes the training data, and its validation loss turns upward (overfitting). A curve that only flattens shows the model has hit the limit of what it can represent. More epochs will not help, because the bottleneck is model capacity, not training time.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the diagnostic. In the universal workflow you first try to build a model that overfits, then regularize it. If you cannot get it to overfit, the next step is to make the model bigger, not to regularize it.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: for a convex model such as logistic regression, the plateau is close to the minimum this model family can reach on this data. The optimizer is not stuck in a bad region; the model family itself is limited.

terminology.meaning: A validation curve that flattens with almost no further improvement.
Validation performance improves to a best point and then gets worse: the U-shaped loss curve typical of overfitting.

p.161: the underfitting/overfitting picture from section 5.1.1

concepts.name: Model capacity (representational power)
concepts.definition: How much information a model can store, and how complex a function it can represent. In practice it is governed by the number of layers, their size (number of parameters), and the types of layers used.
concepts.intuition: Think of capacity as memory size. A tiny model cannot memorize 48,000 training images, so it settles for a coarse rule that works on average.
concepts.technical: A Dense(10) layer on 784 inputs represents only affine maps followed by softmax, so the class boundaries are hyperplanes. Adding hidden layers with nonlinear activations lets the model represent piecewise-linear boundaries of far greater complexity.
concepts.significance: Without enough capacity, a model cannot overfit, and so it also cannot reach the best generalization the data allows.
concepts.example: Listing 5.9 (7,850 parameters) plateaus at a validation loss of about 0.26. The 2×128-unit model on p.181 fits fast and starts overfitting after eight epochs.
concepts.misconception: That a model which never overfits is a well-regularized, healthy model. On this page it is a model that is too weak.

concepts.name: Logistic regression (softmax regression)
concepts.definition: A linear classifier: class scores are an affine function of the input, converted to probabilities by a sigmoid (binary) or softmax (multiclass).
concepts.intuition: Each class gets one 'template' weight image. The input is scored by how well it matches each template.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: $p(y=k\mid x) = \operatorname{softmax}(Wx+b)_k$ with $W\in\mathbb{R}^{10\times 784}$. Trained with crossentropy, the loss is convex in $W, b$.
concepts.significance: It is the simplest neural network: one Dense layer with no hidden layers. That makes it the natural minimal-capacity baseline in Listing 5.9.
concepts.misconception: Despite the name, logistic regression is a classification method, not a regression method.

concepts.name: Underfitting from insufficient capacity
concepts.definition: The model cannot fit the training data well enough to reach the overfitting regime. Training and validation losses both stay relatively high and flatten.
concepts.intuition: The student is not lazy. They simply lack the vocabulary to express the answer.
concepts.technical: The diagnostic is curve shape: a monotone, flattening validation loss with no minimum followed by an increase (Figure 5.14).
concepts.significance: It tells you which way to move: increase capacity before considering regularization.
concepts.example: Validation loss about 0.26 and flat from roughly epoch 12 to 20 in Figure 5.14.
concepts.misconception: That more epochs will fix it. If the curve has flattened, the bottleneck is the model, not training time.

concepts.name: validation_split
concepts.definition: A `fit()` argument that holds out the given fraction of the training arrays, taken from the end of the data before any shuffling, and evaluates on it after each epoch.
concepts.intuition: A built-in mini exam that the model never trains on.
concepts.technical: With `validation_split=0.2` on 60,000 MNIST images, the last 12,000 are held out for validation and 48,000 are used for training. Their metrics are logged as `val_loss` and `val_accuracy`.
concepts.significance: It produces the `val_loss` curve plotted in Figure 5.14, which is the basis of the whole diagnosis.
concepts.misconception: That validation_split picks a random subset. Keras takes the last samples, so ordered data can bias the validation set.

code.title: A simple logistic regression on MNIST
code.original_code:
model = keras.Sequential([layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])
model.compile(
    optimizer="rmsprop",
    loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
history_small_model = model.fit(
    train_images, train_labels, epochs=20, batch_size=128, validation_split=0.2
)
code.what_it_does: Builds a one-layer softmax classifier, compiles it for integer-label multiclass classification, and trains it for 20 epochs on 80% of the MNIST training set while validating on the remaining 20%. The training record is stored in history_small_model.

line_explanations.explanation: A Sequential model with a single Dense layer of 10 units, one per digit class, with a softmax activation. No input shape is given, so the weights are created on the first call (784×10 kernel + 10 biases).
Compile with the RMSprop optimizer, sparse categorical crossentropy (labels are integers 0-9, not one-hot), and an accuracy metric.

Train for 20 epochs with mini-batches of 128. validation_split=0.2 holds out the last 20% of train_images/train_labels. The returned History object's .history dict holds per-epoch loss, accuracy, val_loss and val_accuracy.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: train_images of shape (60000, 784), float in [0, 1], and train_labels of shape (60000,), integer, both prepared earlier in the chapter. Output: a trained model plus history_small_model.history with 20 values per metric.
code.algorithm: Mini-batch gradient descent (RMSprop) on the crossentropy of a linear-softmax model.
code.theory_link: This is the minimal-capacity model used to show the 'cannot overfit' curve of section 5.3.3.

parameters.name: Dense(10, activation="softmax")
parameters.role: The entire model: 7,850 parameters, linear decision boundaries.

parameters.name: epochs=20
parameters.role: Enough passes for a bigger model to overfit. Here it shows the curve has flattened.

parameters.name: validation_split=0.2
parameters.role: Fraction of the training data held out for validation (12,000 images).

pitfalls: train_images must already be flattened to (n, 784). A Dense layer applied to (n, 28, 28) inputs would act only on the last axis and give the wrong output shape.
With one-hot labels you would need categorical_crossentropy instead of the sparse variant.
validation_split takes the tail of the arrays, not a random sample.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: count parameters and inspect the final metrics
model.summary()  # dense: 7,850 params
h = history_small_model.history
print(min(h["val_loss"]), h["val_accuracy"][-1])

code.title: Plotting the validation loss (Figure 5.14)
code.original_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
val_loss = history_small_model.history["val_loss"]
epochs = range(1, 21)
plt.plot(epochs, val_loss, "b-", label="Validation loss")
plt.title("Validation loss for a model with insufficient capacity")
plt.xlabel("Epochs")
plt.ylabel("Loss")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
code.what_it_does: Extracts the per-epoch validation loss from the History object and plots it as a solid blue line against epochs 1-20, producing Figure 5.14.

line_explanations.explanation: history_small_model.history is a dict. The 'val_loss' key holds a list of 20 floats, one per epoch.
'b-' means a blue solid line. label feeds the legend.
Title, axis labels, legend, and display.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the History from Listing 5.9. Output: a line chart.
code.theory_link: The shape of this one curve (flattening, no upturn) is the evidence for insufficient capacity.

parameters.name: "b-"
parameters.role: Matplotlib format string: blue, solid line.

pitfalls: range(1, 21) is hard-coded to 20 epochs. Use range(1, len(val_loss) + 1) if you change epochs.
Plotting only validation loss hides the training loss. Adding it would show how close the two stay, which is another underfitting sign.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: also plot training loss for comparison
plt.plot(epochs, history_small_model.history["loss"], "bo", label="Training loss")

deeper.title: Why the curve flattens instead of turning up
deeper.body:
1. Overfitting means the model starts encoding quirks of individual training samples that do not transfer to new data.
2. Encoding quirks takes free parameters. A linear model with 7,850 weights shared across 48,000 images cannot fit individual examples. It can only learn one template per class.
3. So once the best linear templates are found, nothing more can be learned: training and validation losses both level off.
4. Because softmax regression with crossentropy is convex, this plateau is close to the minimum the model can reach. It is the model family's ceiling, not an optimization failure.

(Beyond the book: points 2-4 are added explanation.)

deeper.title: Template matching analogy
deeper.body: Logistic regression on MNIST is like recognizing digits by laying ten stencils over the image and choosing the one that overlaps best. It works most of the time (about 92% accuracy), but a slanted 7 or an open 4 defeats every stencil. Studying longer does not help; you need a richer recognition method, meaning hidden layers.

deeper.title: Three curve shapes to recognize
deeper.body:
- **Loss does not go down at all**: an optimization problem (learning rate, batch size; p.178-179).
- **Loss goes down, then validation turns up**: overfitting, which is the desired intermediate state. Next, regularize (section 5.4).
- **Loss goes down and flattens without turning up (this page)**: insufficient capacity. Next, increase model size (p.181).

misconceptions.claim: A validation loss that never increases means the model generalizes perfectly.
misconceptions.correction: Here it means the model is too small to overfit. Its validation loss (about 0.26) is far worse than what a bigger model reaches before overfitting.

misconceptions.claim: Training longer will eventually push the loss down further.
misconceptions.correction: The curve has already flattened by about epoch 12. The limit is capacity, not training time.

misconceptions.claim: Logistic regression is a regression model.
misconceptions.correction: It is a classifier: a linear model with sigmoid/softmax outputs trained with crossentropy.

takeaways: Dense(10, softmax) on raw pixels is a logistic regression: 7,850 parameters and linear decision boundaries.
Its validation loss falls to about 0.26 and plateaus. It never peaks and reverses.
A curve that cannot overfit signals insufficient capacity, not good regularization.
validation_split=0.2 plus the History object give you the curves you need for this diagnosis.
The remedy, given on p.181, is more representational power.

questions.question: What shape of validation-loss curve does the book associate with insufficient model capacity?
options: It stalls or improves very slowly without reversing course
It stays flat at the random-guess level from the first epoch
It oscillates wildly from epoch to epoch
questions.answer: It stalls or improves very slowly without reversing course
questions.explanation: Figure 5.14 flattens around 0.26. An upturn is overfitting. A loss stuck at chance level points to an unsolvable problem or a bad architecture prior (p.179). Wild oscillation suggests too high a learning rate.

questions.question: Why is the model in Listing 5.9 a logistic regression?
questions.answer: It is a single Dense layer mapping inputs linearly to 10 scores, followed by softmax: a linear model with softmax probabilities, trained with crossentropy.
questions.explanation: With no hidden layers there is no nonlinearity before the softmax, so it is exactly multinomial logistic regression.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does Listing 5.9's model have on flattened 28×28 MNIST images?
questions.explanation: The kernel has 784×10 weights and there is one bias per unit.

questions.question: With validation_split=0.2 on the 60,000 MNIST training images, how many images are used for training and how many for validation?
questions.answer: 48,000 for training and 12,000 for validation (the last 20% of the arrays).
questions.explanation: Keras slices off the final fraction of the arrays as validation data before training.

questions.question: Why should you not just train Listing 5.9's model for 200 epochs instead of 20?
questions.answer: The validation loss has already plateaued. The limit is the model's representational power, so more epochs give essentially nothing; you need a bigger model.
questions.explanation: The text notes that you cannot clearly overfit 'even after many iterations' (continued on p.181).

questions.question: Why is 'cannot overfit' a problem rather than a good thing?
questions.answer: A model that cannot overfit lacks the capacity to capture all the useful structure in the data. You want to reach the overfitting regime, then pull back with regularization, so you find the best trade-off.
questions.explanation: The book's position (p.181) is that it should always be possible to overfit, and failing to do so means you need more capacity.

questions.question: Can you sketch, from memory, the three validation curves for a model with too little, appropriate, and too much capacity?
questions.answer: Too little: drops and flattens (Fig. 5.14). Appropriate: drops, reaches a minimum around epoch 8, then rises (Fig. 5.15). Too much: rises almost immediately (Fig. 5.16).
questions.explanation: These three figures form the comparison running through pp.180-182.
